subject: Isaac the Syrian (Isaac of Nineveh), 7th-century monk, bishop of Nineveh for five months, hermit and writer

text_used.text: Isaac's own words are checked against A. J. Wensinck's English translation from the Syriac, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh (Amsterdam, 1923). Public domain: published 1923 and Wensinck died in 1939. Three copies were fetched and checked: the Commons PDF (a photographic 1969 reprint of the 1923 edition, which also holds Wensinck's Preface and Introduction with his English of the two early notices on Isaac's life), and the two archive.org OCR texts (which lack the Introduction). 'exact' is the translation as printed, with footnote marks and Bedjan's margin page numbers taken out and the typesetter's space before ';' ':' '?' closed up. 'display' applies the site's rule of capitals for every pronoun for God. 'place' gives the chapter in the Syriac numbering (Bedjan and Wensinck), which is the numbering in the Syriac and in Wensinck; the Greek and the Holy Transfiguration Monastery English number the homilies differently.
text_used.source: A. J. Wensinck (tr.), Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh, translated from Bedjan's Syriac text (Amsterdam: Royal Academy, 1923); Commons PDF of the 1969 photographic reprint, and the archive.org scans
text_used.note: Wensinck calls the 82 pieces 'treatises' in his Introduction and 'chapters' in his table of contents. The usual English name for the book is 'Ascetical Homilies' (the name of the 1984 Holy Transfiguration Monastery translation from the Greek, copyrighted). Page URLs use the PDF's own page numbers: Wensinck's page N is PDF page N+56. The archive.org copy uploaded by Roger Pearse is marked CC BY 3.0 by the uploader, but the translation itself is public domain. The Commons file page tags the scan PD-old-70 + Public Domain Mark (checked).

the_two_early_notices.text: Almost everything known of Isaac's life comes from two short notices. (1) Isho'dnah of Basra's Book of Chastity (9th century; Syriac edited with French by J.-B. Chabot in 1896). (2) An anonymous West Syrian notice printed by I. E. Rahmani in Studia Syriaca. Wensinck translates both into English in his Introduction (pages XVIII-XIX). Isaac says very little about himself in his own book.
the_two_early_notices.source: Wensinck, Mystic Treatises (1923), Introduction, page XVIII, his English of the notice in Isho'dnah of Basra's Book of Chastity (9th century; Syriac ed. J.-B. Chabot, 1896); Wensinck, Mystic Treatises (1923), Introduction, pages XVIII-XIX, his English of the anonymous West Syrian notice printed by Rahmani in Studia Syriaca; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('Since the discovery of Ishodenah's "Book of Chastity" by Chabot in 1895 the above details of Isaac's life are beyond doubt'); e-GEDSH ('as one of the two short biographical accounts puts it')
the_two_early_notices.note: Isho'dnah's heading: 'On the holy Mar Isaac, bishop of Ninive, who resigned his episcopal office and wrote books on the behaviour of solitaries.' Wensinck: 'Isaac very seldom speaks plainly about himself; he usually imitates the way in which St. Paul once speaks about his own experiences: I know a man who etc.' (Introduction, pages XIX-XX).

born_year.text: Not recorded. Neither notice gives a year. He was made bishop between 676 and 680 and died 'in high age', so he was born in the first half of the 7th century, but no source fixes it.
born_year.source: Isho'dnah and the West Syrian notice (Wensinck, Introduction, pages XVIII-XIX); Holy See Press Office, 9 November 2024 ('between 676 and 680'); e-GEDSH ('perhaps ca. 676/80')
born_year.note: Wikipedia's 'c. 613' has no source I could find, and Wikidata's '640' is unverified (people-audit.json). Do not print a birth year. 'First half of the 7th century' is our own inference from the dates of his episcopate and his old age; say 'born in the 600s' or leave the year out.

born_place.text: Born in Beth Qatraye, the Syriac name for the Gulf coast of north-eastern Arabia with Qatar at its heart. The Vatican says 'present-day Qatar'.
born_place.source: Isho'dnah ('He was born in Bet Ḳaṭrāyē'); West Syrian notice ('born in Bet Ḳaṭrāyē beneath India'); e-GEDSH, 'Beth Qaṭraye' (the region includes Qatar, its hinterland Yamama, 'the entire coast of northeast Arabia as far as the peninsula of Musandam' and the islands); Holy See Press Office 2024 ('Born in present-day Qatar')
born_place.note: Plain wording that holds: 'Born in Beth Qatraye, on the Gulf coast of Arabia (today Qatar and its neighbours).' Brock calls him 'Isaac of Beth Qatraye' in the title of one article (e-GEDSH bibliography). Britannica's 'a monk of Bet-Qatraje in Kurdistan' is a mistake (see misquoted_or_legend).

grew_up.text: In Beth Qatraye. He studied the Scriptures and their commentaries there, became a monk and taught in his own country.
grew_up.source: West Syrian notice (Wensinck, Introduction, page XVIII)
grew_up.note: Exact: 'When he had become excercised in the writings of the Church and their commentaries he became a monk and a teacher in his country.' Nothing is recorded of his parents. The West Syrian notice says he was 'a relative of Mar Gabriel Ḳaṭrāyā, the commentator of the church'. Isaac mentions a 'natural and spiritual brother' who was also a monk (chapter 42).

died.text: Around 700, in old age and blind, at the monastery of Rabban Shabur in Beth Huzaye (Khuzistan, south-west Iran). No day or year is recorded. The notices say only that he died 'in high age'.
died.source: Isho'dnah ('In high age he departed this temporary life'); West Syrian notice ('When he had grown old and had reached a high age, he departed unto our Lord'); Britannica ('died c. 700, near Susa'); e-GEDSH (the monastery was 'in the region of Shuster'); Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('died at an advanced age, blind through study and austerity')
died.note: Cause: old age is all the sources say. 'c. 700' is Britannica's estimate. Shuster is Shushtar in Khuzestan province, Iran; Britannica's 'near Susa' is the same area, about 60 km away (distance not checked).

buried.text: In the monastery of Rabban Shabur, where he died.
buried.source: Isho'dnah ('his corpse was interred in the monastery of Shabūr'); West Syrian notice ('he was buried in the monastery of Mar Shabūr')
buried.note: No grave or relics are known today (I found no source for any).

also_called.text: Isaac of Nineveh (Catholic usage and scholars: 'St Isaac of Nineveh'). Syriac: Mar Isḥaq of Nineveh.
also_called.source: Holy See Press Office 2024 ('Isaac of Nineveh, also known as Isaac the Syrian'); e-GEDSH ('Isḥaq of Nineveh'); Isho'dnah ('the holy Mar Isaac, bishop of Ninive')
also_called.note: Search demand splits between 'Isaac of Nineveh' and 'Isaac the Syrian' (SEARCH-BRIEF). Use both on the page.

also_called.text: Isaac the Syrian (Orthodox usage in English). OCA: 'Saint Isaac the Syrian, Bishop of Nineveh'.
Russian: Isaac Sirin, 'Venerable Isaac the Syrian, of Nineveh, bishop' (Prepodobny Isaak Sirin, Nineviysky).
also_called.note: 'Sirin' means 'the Syrian'. The Commons pictures are titled 'Isaac Sirin'.

also_called.text: Greek: Osios Isaak o Syros, 'Saint (Venerable) Isaac the Syrian'; also 'Abba Isaac' (Abbas Isaak).
also_called.source: saint.gr ('Όσιος Ισαάκ ο Σύρος'); OrthoChristian (Paisios: 'read Abba Isaac')

also_called.text: Latin and Italian printed books: 'Isaac de Syria', 'Abbate Ysaac' (Abbot Isaac).
also_called.source: Commons, 'Isaac - De perfectione vitae theoreticae, 1500' (BEIC record: author 'Isaac : de Syria'; the woodcut is labelled 'Abbate Ysaac'); L'Osservatore Romano 2025 (the Latin book 'attribuito all'“abate Isacco”')

also_called.text: 'The second Didymus': a nickname his brethren gave him, according to the West Syrian notice.
also_called.note: 'because he was placid and kind and humble, and his speech was meek'.

status.text: Saint in the Orthodox Church ('Venerable', a monk-saint). Added to the Catholic Church's Roman Martyrology in 2024. In life, a bishop of the Church of the East, the church of the Persian Empire that did not accept the Council of Ephesus (431).
status.source: OCA; azbyka.ru; saint.gr; Pope Francis, address of 9 November 2024; Holy See Press Office, 9 November 2024; Isho'dnah (ordained by 'Mar George the Katholikos', head of the Church of the East)
status.note: Short form for the sheet: 'Saint, Orthodox and Catholic. A bishop of the Church of the East.' See is_he_a_saint for each church and the old dispute over the word 'Nestorian'.

patron_of.text: None found. No church source names him patron of anything.
patron_of.source: OCA, azbyka.ru, saint.gr, Holy See 2024, Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 (none gives a patronage)

in_art.text: In Russian manuscripts and icons: an old monk with a long grey beard and a halo, standing and holding an open scroll (the 1518 miniature), or seated at a desk writing in a book (an icon dated 1802 on Commons).
in_art.source: The pictures themselves: Commons 'Isaac Sirin miniature.jpg' (1518) and 'Isaac Sirin.jpg' (1802)
in_art.note: Observed from the pictures only; no reference work on his iconography checked. The scroll in the 1518 miniature seems to carry the opening words of his own book (my reading of the Slavonic: 'Strakh Bozhii nachalo dobrodeteli ...', 'The fear of God is the beginning of virtue'; Wensinck's English of the first line: 'The fear of God is the foundation of excellence'). Not checked by a Slavonist.

in_art.text: In the West he has almost no art of his own. The 1500 Venice printing of his book shows 'Abbate Ysaac' as a hooded, bearded abbot with a tau cross on his habit, a staff with a small bell, and a pig at his feet: the usual signs of St Antony the Great.
in_art.source: The woodcut itself (Commons, BEIC copy); the Antony attributes: Britannica and Catholic Encyclopedia as recorded in research/people/antony-the-great-facts.json (in_art)
in_art.note: That the printer borrowed Antony's look is our observation, not a source's claim: say 'dressed with the signs usually given to St Antony'.

wrote.text: Books of short discourses for monks living alone, in Syriac. Three 'Parts' are known today: the First Part (82 chapters), which was translated into Greek and read everywhere; a Second Part (41 chapters), found in a single early manuscript; and a Third Part (17 chapters), found in a manuscript in Tehran copied about 1900. A letter, prayers and short sayings sit inside them.
wrote.source: e-GEDSH (Brock): 'The First Part, with 82 chapters ... A Second Part, consisting of 41 chapters ... A Third Part ... contains 17 chapters, two of which are duplicates with the First Part, and one with the Second Part.' Wensinck, Introduction, page XIV ('the 82 treatises of the Syriac text')
wrote.note: Old counts differ: the West Syrian notice says 'five volumes'; 'Abdisho' (d. 1318) says 'seven books on the spiritual and divine Sacraments, and one on the Distribution of Food' (Badger 1852, page 370). Britannica's 'only 82 chapters ... survive' is out of date.

pronounced.text: EYE-zik the SEER-ee-un. Also: EYE-zik of NIN-uh-vuh.
pronounced.note: Three MW entries fetched (Isaac, Syrian, Nineveh). The respelling is ours, built from them.

roles.text: Monk and teacher: in Beth Qatraye, his home country on the Gulf.
roles.source: West Syrian notice ('he became a monk and a teacher in his country')

roles.text: Bishop of Nineveh: ordained by the Catholicos George between 676 and 680. He gave it up after five months.
roles.source: Isho'dnah; West Syrian notice; Holy See 2024 ('between 676 and 680')
roles.note: Nineveh lay across the Tigris from today's Mosul (Vatican: 'near present-day Mosul (Iraq)').

roles.text: Hermit: in the mountains of Beth Huzaye (Khuzistan), 'among the anchorites who were there'.
roles.source: Isho'dnah ('the mountain of Matūt which surrounds Bēt Huzājē'); West Syrian notice ('the Mountain of Bet Huzāyē')

roles.text: Writer: at the monastery of Rabban Shabur, where he went blind and the brothers wrote down his teaching.
roles.source: Isho'dnah; West Syrian notice ('At last he became blind, so that the brethren wrote down his doctrine')

orthodox_oca.source: OCA, Lives of the Saints ('Commemorated on January 28')
orthodox_oca.note: The OCA lists him with Ephrem the Syrian on 28 January. The OCA's 28 September list does not include him (checked).

orthodox_russian.text: 28 January on the old (Julian) calendar, which is 10 February on the civil calendar.
orthodox_russian.source: azbyka.ru ('День памяти: 10 февраля'; azbyka's 10 February 2026 page lists him)
orthodox_russian.note: The +13 days rule: 28 January Julian = 10 February Gregorian.

orthodox_greek.text: 28 September (Mount Athos and Greek calendars today). Before that he was remembered on 28 January with Ephrem the Syrian.
orthodox_greek.source: saint.gr ('Εορτάζει στις 28 Σεπτεμβρίου εκάστου έτους'); Metropolis of Nea Ionia (nif.gr, same text); OrthoChristian ('Today the feast of St. Isaac is celebrated on Mount Athos on September 28th')
orthodox_greek.note: GOARCH blocked the checker (HTTP 403), as for Martin and Antony. synaxarion.gr's day pages did not return content to the checker.

why_two_orthodox_dates.text: He had no fixed day in the Greek calendar and was named on 28 January beside Ephrem. St Paisios of Mount Athos, who loved his writings, had a service written for him and chose 28 September.
why_two_orthodox_dates.source: saint.gr and nif.gr ('Δεν είχε καθορισμένη ημερομηνία εορτασμού'; 'με πρωτοβουλία του οσίου γέροντος Παϊσίου'); OrthoChristian (the service by the hymnographer Gerasimos Mikragiannanitis)
why_two_orthodox_dates.note: OrthoChristian says the Slavic churches keep 28 January 'officially'.

catholic.text: In the Roman Martyrology since 2024: Pope Francis announced his inclusion on 9 November 2024. The official texts name no day. He is not on the General Roman Calendar (no Mass memorial).
catholic.source: Pope Francis, address to Mar Awa III, 9 November 2024; Holy See Press Office, same day; Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, 11 November 2024
catholic.note: Many websites give 28 January for the Catholic day; I found no published Martyrology entry or decree with a date. Print 'Roman Martyrology (added 2024)' without a day until one is found. 28 January is also St Thomas Aquinas's memorial in the General Roman Calendar.

church_of_the_east.text: His own church. He was one of its bishops, and the Assyrian Church of the East gave its agreement to his entry in the Roman Martyrology. Its day for him was not verified.
church_of_the_east.source: Isho'dnah (ordained by the Catholicos George); Pope Francis 2024 ('with the agreement of Your Holiness and the Patriarch of the Chaldean Church'); Assyrian Church News (a monastery of St Isaac of Nineveh opened by Mar Awa Royel in California)
church_of_the_east.note: Leave the Church of the East's date blank.

anglican_episcopal_lutheran.text: Not kept. He is not in the Church of England's Common Worship calendar, the Episcopal Church's Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, the ELCA's Evangelical Lutheran Worship list, or the LCMS Lutheran Service Book list.
anglican_episcopal_lutheran.source: Church of England calendar page (saved by the Antony researcher; searched: no Isaac but Isaac Watts); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 full text (searched: only Samuel Isaac Joseph Schereschewsky); ELW 2006 calendar PDF (only Isaac Watts); LCMS/CPH commemorations list (only the patriarch Isaac, 16 August)
anglican_episcopal_lutheran.note: Say so plainly: 'Not in the Anglican or Lutheran calendars.'

numbers.label: Months as bishop
numbers.text: He was bishop of Nineveh for five months, then gave it up.
numbers.source: Isho'dnah ('for five months'); West Syrian notice ('for five months only')

numbers.label: Chapters in his great book
numbers.text: The First Part of his writings has 82 chapters. It is the book the Greek, Russian and Latin worlds read.
numbers.note: Wensinck: 14 of the 82 are missing from the Greek translation.

numbers.label: Loaves a week
numbers.text: He ate only three loaves of bread a week, with a few vegetables, and never tasted cooked food.

numbers.label: Parts of his writings
numbers.text: Three Parts of his writings are known today: 82, 41 and 17 chapters. The second and third were found in modern times.
numbers.note: The date the Second Part was found (often given as 1983) is not verified here.

numbers.label: Latin manuscripts
numbers.text: More than sixty manuscripts survive of the Latin translation made around 1200.

numbers.label: Year Rome added him
numbers.text: The Catholic Church added him to the Roman Martyrology in 2024, some 1,300 years after his death.

traits.text: He taught that a pure heart is a heart full of mercy for all that God made. It weeps for people, birds, beasts, reptiles, enemies and even demons.

quote.exact: And what is a merciful heart? He replied: The burning of the heart unto the whole creation, man, fowls and beasts, demons and whatever exists; so that by the recollection and the sight of them the eyes shed tears on account of the force of mercy which moves the heart by great compassion.

traits.text: His brothers called him 'the second Didymus' for his gentleness. He said he had not lived a thousandth of what he wrote.

quote.exact: At last he became blind, so that the brethren wrote down his doctrine. They gave him the surname of the second Didymus, because he was placid and kind and humble, and his speech was meek. He ate only three loafs of bread a week, with small vegetables; he never tasted what was cooked. He wrote five volumes which are extant till now [full of] sweet doctrine.

traits.text: Three loaves a week, no cooked food, and reading until he went blind. He even refused to visit his own brother, a fellow monk, who begged to see him.

quote.exact: Do not ask from me, o my brother, what gives consolation to body and mind, but let me seek the salvation of my soul. Yet a short time and we shall have passed away from this world.

also.exact: Afterwards he went to the monastery of Rabban Shabūr and became exceedingly well acquainted with the divine writings; at last he lost his eyesight through his reading and asceticism. He penetrated deeply into the divine mysteries and wrote books on the divine behaviour of solitaries. He said three things which were not accepted by the community. Daniel, the bishop of Bet Garmaia, was scandalized at him on account of these things which he said. In high age he departed this temporary life; his corpse was interred in the monastery of Shabūr.

life_moments.place: Beth Qatraye (today Qatar and the Gulf coast)
life_moments.title: A monk and teacher on the Gulf
life_moments.story: Isaac was born in Beth Qatraye, on the Arabian shore of the Gulf. He studied the Scriptures and their commentaries, became a monk, and taught in his own country. He was related to Gabriel of Qatar, a known Bible commentator.
life_moments.source: West Syrian notice (Wensinck, Introduction, page XVIII); Isho'dnah ('He was born in Bet Ḳaṭrāyē'); e-GEDSH 'Beth Qaṭraye'

life_moments.title: The Catholicos takes him north
life_moments.story: George, the head of the Church of the East, came to Beth Qatraye. When he went home he took Isaac with him to Beth Aramaye, in today's Iraq.
life_moments.source: West Syrian notice ('when Mar George the Katholikos went to his own country, he took Isaac with him to Bet Aramāyē'); e-GEDSH 'Beth Qaṭraye' (George's synod in Beth Qatraye in 676; 'before Cath. Gewargis took him to Beth Aramaye')

life_moments.place: Monastery of Beth Abe, then Nineveh (by today's Mosul)
life_moments.title: Bishop for five months
life_moments.story: George ordained him bishop of Nineveh in the monastery of Beth Abe, as successor to Bishop Moses. Five months later he gave it up 'for a reason which God knows' and went to live in the mountains. The West Syrian notice says his 'keen mind' and 'zeal' could not endure the work. In his own book a hermit, whom Wensinck takes to be Isaac, asks God whether grace left him 'on account of my episcopal rank'. The answer: in the desert God fed you; in the city, men do.
life_moments.source: Isho'dnah (Wensinck, page XVIII); West Syrian notice (page XIX); Ascetical Homilies, chapter 35 (Wensinck page 167); Holy See 2024 ('between 676 and 680')

life_moments.place: Mar Saba, near Jerusalem; then the whole Church
life_moments.title: The book that crossed every border
life_moments.story: Two monks of the Greek monastery of Mar Saba translated most of his First Part into Greek in the late 8th or early 9th century. From Greek it went into Slavonic, Arabic, Georgian and Latin. A Latin version from around 1200 survives in more than sixty manuscripts, and an Italian version was printed at Venice in 1500. In Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov (1880) a servant reads 'the God-fearing Father Isaac the Syrian' for years. In 2024 the Catholic Church added him to its Martyrology.

evidence.exact: And what is a merciful heart? He replied: The burning of the heart unto the whole creation, man, fowls and beasts, demons and whatever exists; so that by the recollection and the sight of them the eyes shed tears on account of the force of mercy which moves the heart by great compassion. Then the heart becomes weak and it is not able to bear hearing or examining injury or any insignificant suffering of anything in the creation. hard_question.text: Was he a 'Nestorian'? He was a bishop of the Church of the East, which rejected the Council of Ephesus and was called 'Nestorian' by its rivals. The 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia calls him 'A Nestorian bishop' and thinks his disputed theses were 'too Catholic'. Some Orthodox, following St Paisios, hold that he was fully Orthodox and fought Nestorianism. The Vatican in 2024 simply said he belonged to 'a Church that was no longer in communion with any other'. He praises Theodore of Mopsuestia as 'the light of the whole world', and Wensinck notes one passage in the Syriac that 'looks like a Nestorian addition' and is missing from the Greek.
hard_question.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910; Holy See Press Office 2024; OrthoChristian (Paisios); Ascetical Homilies, chapter 19 (Wensinck page 105) and Wensinck's footnote in chapter 33, page 149 ('The passage is lacking in the Greek translation and looks like a Nestorian addition')
hard_question.note: State both sides in their own words. Avoid the word 'Nestorian' in our own voice: say 'the Church of the East'.

hard_topics.text: His church: see is_he_a_saint.hard_question. State both the 'Church of the East bishop' view (the notices, e-GEDSH, the Vatican) and the Orthodox view that he was fully Orthodox (Paisios), in their own words.

Hell and hope for all. In the First Part he says sin 'will not be', that hell's 'end is not known', and that the damned are 'tormented with the scourgings of love'. His Second Part (Syriac, found in modern times; English by S. Brock, 1995, CSCO 224-225, copyrighted) argues more openly that Gehenna will end. The qualifying voice: Metropolitan Hilarion Alfeyev, who does not doubt Isaac hoped all would be saved, distinguishes it from Origen's apokatastasis (condemned at the Fifth Council, 553), and writes: 'The teaching on universal salvation, which is so explicitly preached by Isaac the Syrian, has never been approved by the Orthodox Church.'
hard_topics.source: Ascetical Homilies, chapters 26 and 27 (Wensinck pages 128, 136); Hilarion Alfeyev, St Isaac the Syrian, a Theologian of Love and Mercy (paper, World Congress on Divine Mercy, Lateran Basilica, Rome, 4 April 2008), section Eschatology, as reproduced by Richard Beck (Experimental Theology, 30 January 2020); Brock 1995 edition named in e-GEDSH (Ishaq of Nineveh, bibliography)
hard_topics.note: First Part lines verified in Wensinck. Alfeyev sentence verified word for word in sources/people/isaac-the-syrian/alfeyev-2008-theologian-of-love-and-mercy.txt (copyrighted; one sentence quoted, fair use). His calling Isaac one of the greatest theologians of the Orthodox tradition and the Fifth Council point are paraphrased from the same paper. The Second Part itself is still not fetched: do not quote it. Do not say the three things Daniel objected to were about hell: no source says so.

hard_topics.text: Harsh with himself and with monks: fasting 'feeding upon drugs and dry stubble'; refusing to visit a dying brother ('should I then honour nature above Christ?'); telling a solitary his 'rank is higher than that of almsgivers'. The balance, in his own words: a hermit who walks past a sick brother 'pretending a sham solitude ... is without mercy'.

Page 1 (1920px rendering) re-read by eye: the caption under the frontispiece says it is an exact copy of the picture of St Isaac the Syrian in a Slavonic manuscript of his works kept in the library of the monastery of St Sabbas the Sanctified and written in 1359 on Mount Athos, in the Lavra of St Athanasius, as the manuscript's inscription says. The stamp zone was compared with the scan: the round Perm University stamp on the blank paper is gone, the frame's left border and the cloak are intact. A different work from the band (1518 Russian miniature) and the portrait (1500 Venice woodcut). File on disk 678 x 1210, as the data says.
